title: Regime shift

definition.text: A large, abrupt and lasting change in how an ecosystem, the climate, a financial system or another complex system is structured and works.

facts.text: A regime is a typical behaviour of a system held in place by mutually reinforcing feedbacks.
Shifts happen when stabilising feedbacks weaken or an external shock exceeds the system's capacity to absorb it.
Regime shifts matter in ecology because they can sharply change the flow of ecosystem services such as food, clean water and climate regulation.
They are hard to reverse and sometimes irreversible.
A small disturbance can produce big effects, so inputs and outputs are not proportional.
Regime shifts are expected to become more common as human influence on the planet grows.
Strong evidence emerged in the 1990s from kelp forests, coral reefs, drylands and shallow lakes.
Deforestation could shift Amazon and East Asian rainforests toward savanna, affecting food, fresh water, climate regulation and biodiversity.

related: Tipping points in the climate system
contested_note: There is no agreed definition, and how the concept should be applied remains contested.

definition.text: Three patterns of change in systems prone to regime shifts, set by how fast and slow processes interact.

facts.text: Smooth change follows a nearly straight-line relationship between slow and fast variables; abrupt change follows a non-linear one.
In discontinuous change the system flips back at a different point from where it flipped forward, which is hysteresis.
Woody plant encroachment on drylands, where small changes in grazing shift grassland to woody savanna, is thought to be a smooth-change case.

title: Detecting regime shifts
article: Regime shift#Detection of whether a regime shift has occurred

definition.text: Statistical ways of telling from data whether a system has already shifted regime.

facts.text: Methods such as principal component analysis or neural networks need long data series and only work after the threshold is crossed.
Failing to find multiple regimes in data does not rule out a future shift.
For managers, assuming a system has only one regime can be risky when the alternatives are very harmful.

title: Alternative stable state

definition.text: The ecological theory that an ecosystem can settle into more than one stable state under the same conditions.

facts.text: A move between states, called a state shift, phase shift or regime shift, happens when the ecosystem is perturbed.
Feedbacks make ecosystems resist shifting, so they stay in one state unless the push is large enough.
Discrete states are separated by ecological thresholds, unlike ecosystems that change smoothly along a gradient.
Richard Lewontin first proposed the theory in 1969.
Coral reefs can flip from coral-dominated to degraded algae-dominated systems when algae grazers decline.
A 2005 review found 21 valid direct experiments, of which 14 supported alternative stable states and 8 did not.
If stable states exist, gradual change may have little effect until a threshold triggers a catastrophic shift, which matters for monitoring and restoration.

title: Ball-and-cup model

definition.text: A picture of ecosystem states as a ball rolling on a landscape of valleys and hills.

facts.text: In the simplest version two valleys are separated by a hill; a ball in a valley sits in a stable state, or domain of attraction.
Moving the ball to another valley takes enough force to push it over the hill.
A steep-sided valley is more resilient than a shallow one.

distinct_from: Community and ecosystem perspectives on state shifts

title: Community and ecosystem perspectives on state shifts

definition.text: Two explanations of state shifts: pushing fast-changing state variables directly, or changing slow parameters that reshape the landscape of states.

facts.text: State variables, such as population densities, respond quickly to system feedbacks; parameters respond slowly or not at all.
In the community view the landscape is fixed; in the ecosystem view environmental drivers change the number, location and resilience of stable states.

title: Human erosion of ecosystem resilience

definition.text: The ways human activity makes stable ecosystem states easier to tip into worse ones.

facts.text: People reduce resilience by cutting diversity (as in overfishing), altering the physical and chemical environment, and changing disturbance regimes such as through bottom trawling.
With less resilience, minor perturbations can push ecosystems into less desirable states.
Such shifts often lose ecosystem services and have been documented on land, at sea and in fresh water.

distinct_from: Community and ecosystem perspectives on state shifts

title: Balance of nature

definition.text: The idea that ecosystems naturally sit in a stable equilibrium, with small changes corrected by negative feedback.

facts.text: The idea is ancient: Herodotus, Plato and Cicero all described a balance in nature.
It once governed ecological research and natural resource management, and was a central theme of Rachel Carson's 1962 Silent Spring.
Ecologists abandoned it in the late 20th century because constant disturbance and chaotic change turned out to be the norm.
An eight-year study of isolated Baltic plankton showed species populations rising and falling chaotically even under constant conditions.
Many habitats were shaped by people, such as Aboriginal fire-stick farming in Australia.
The idea remains popular with the public, conservationists and environmental groups.

contested_note: Ecologists have discredited the theory, yet some still call it a foundational metaphor and it stays popular with the public.
